raw_evidence.label: Planned obsolescence: the cultural backdrop
raw_evidence.content: Planned obsolescence is the design strategy of building products with artificially short lifespans — through fragile components, software-locked spare parts, glued-shut shells, or proprietary screws — so that consumers replace rather than repair. It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.content: Across all 178,749 logged attempts, volunteers fully repaired the item 63.1% of the time (112,776 cases), partly repaired 12.8% (22,859), and could not repair 24.1% (43,112). This is slightly under the 65% headline statistic the foundation reported in 2018 for fully-successful repairs, suggesting Repair Cafes have, if anything, become slightly more successful over time as volunteer experience accumulates.

raw_evidence.label: Success rate by product type — knives and trousers thrive, kettles and printers don't
raw_evidence.content: Repair success varies wildly by item. The clear winners are non-electric, mechanical items: knives/scissors are repaired 97.5% of the time (mostly sharpening), trousers/pants 96.0%, garden shears 95.4%, coats/jackets 89.7%, and bicycles 84.1%. The clear losers are electronics with sealed components or cheap consumer-grade builds: electric kettles succeed only 39.9% (50.9% are unfixable), printers 36.8% (42.2% unfixable), irons 49.4%, food processors 49.1%, laptops 49.7%, toasters 51.1%, and coffee makers 50.6%. The data tells a story: the more electronic the item, the less likely it can be saved.
raw_evidence.code:
ct = pd.crosstab(sub['kind_of_product'], sub['repaired'], normalize='index') * 100
ct = ct.reindex(top20)
ct['n'] = repairs['kind_of_product'].value_counts().reindex(top20).values
print(ct.round(1).to_string())

# --- ana_05: Country distribution ---
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
country_counts = repairs['country'].value_counts()

raw_evidence.label: Category-level repair odds: textile thrives, electronics struggle
raw_evidence.content: Aggregating to the 14 high-level categories, textile leads on repair success at 92.3% (24,412 rows), followed by tools non-electric (90.0%) and jewelry (82.9%). At the bottom, display-and-sound equipment is repaired only 45.8% of the time (20,415 rows) and computer-equipment-and-phones 46.4% (9,488 rows). Household appliances electric, the largest category at 70,983 rows, sits at 55.3% — almost exactly mid-pack. The cleanest split in the data is electric vs non-electric: electric items succeed roughly half the time, non-electric items roughly nine times in ten.

This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.label: Success rate by product type — knives and trousers thrive, kettles and printers don't
raw_evidence.content: Repair success varies wildly by item. The clear winners are non-electric, mechanical items: knives/scissors are repaired 97.5% of the time (mostly sharpening), trousers/pants 96.0%, garden shears 95.4%, coats/jackets 89.7%, and bicycles 84.1%. The clear losers are electronics with sealed components or cheap consumer-grade builds: electric kettles succeed only 39.9% (50.9% are unfixable), printers 36.8% (42.2% unfixable), irons 49.4%, food processors 49.1%, laptops 49.7%, toasters 51.1%, and coffee makers 50.6%. The data tells a story: the more electronic the item, the less likely it can be saved.
raw_evidence.code:
ct = pd.crosstab(sub['kind_of_product'], sub['repaired'], normalize='index') * 100
ct = ct.reindex(top20)
ct['n'] = repairs['kind_of_product'].value_counts().reindex(top20).values
print(ct.round(1).to_string())

# --- ana_05: Country distribution ---
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
country_counts = repairs['country'].value_counts()

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Martine Postma's Amsterdam experiment, October 2009
raw_evidence.content: The first Repair Cafe was held on 18 October 2009 in the Fijnhout Theater in Amsterdam-West, organized by Dutch journalist Martine Postma. After the birth of her second child she became preoccupied with how much serviceable stuff Europeans throw away, and decided to test a simple idea: invite neighbors to bring broken household items to a community space where volunteer fixers help them repair the item, free of charge, over coffee. On 2 March 2010 the Repair Cafe Foundation was set up to professionalize the model and license a starter kit (manuals, posters, tool lists, public liability advice) to local groups in the Netherlands and abroad. By 2025 the movement had spread to more than 40 countries on six continents, with nearly 3,200 active branches; this dataset is the digital exhaust of that grassroots experiment.

raw_evidence.label: What Repair Monitor is, and why this dataset exists
raw_evidence.content: Repair Monitor (dashboard.repairmonitor.org) is the Repair Cafe Foundation's voluntary data-collection arm. Volunteers at participating cafes log each repair attempt: what the item was, who made it, the year, what was wrong, what they did, and whether it ended up repaired, half-repaired, or unfixable. The dashboard aggregates these logs into eight public visualizations showing the most-presented products and brands, participating cafes, and reasons repairs failed. The 2018 Repair Monitor analysis reported a 65% repair success rate and noted that in 46% of unsuccessful cases the blocker was a non-replaceable broken part. The TidyTuesday 2026 release exposes the raw row-level data behind that dashboard for the first time, including the long free-text fields (defect_found, problem_description, failure_reason_open, suggestions) that volunteers wrote in their own words.

raw_evidence.label: Yearly volume: 1,600x growth from 2015 to 2025
raw_evidence.content: Logged repairs grew from 28 in 2015 (the dashboard's first year) to 45,165 in 2025 — a 1,613x increase. Growth was steady through 2019 (15,491 logs), dropped to 6,686 in 2020 and 5,813 in 2021 (COVID closed cafes physically), then rebounded in 2022 (15,096) and accelerated to 29,406 (2023), 39,981 (2024), and 45,165 (2025). The 2026 figure of 7,346 reflects only the first eight months. The reach of the Repair Cafe movement, in other words, is a hockey stick — the data underestimates the early years because the dashboard didn't exist yet.

By 2025 the movement had spread to more than 40 countries on six continents, with nearly 3,200 active branches; this dataset is the digital exhaust of that grassroots experiment.

raw_evidence.label: What Repair Monitor is, and why this dataset exists
raw_evidence.content: Repair Monitor (dashboard.repairmonitor.org) is the Repair Cafe Foundation's voluntary data-collection arm. Volunteers at participating cafes log each repair attempt: what the item was, who made it, the year, what was wrong, what they did, and whether it ended up repaired, half-repaired, or unfixable. The dashboard aggregates these logs into eight public visualizations showing the most-presented products and brands, participating cafes, and reasons repairs failed. The 2018 Repair Monitor analysis reported a 65% repair success rate and noted that in 46% of unsuccessful cases the blocker was a non-replaceable broken part. The TidyTuesday 2026 release exposes the raw row-level data behind that dashboard for the first time, including the long free-text fields (defect_found, problem_description, failure_reason_open, suggestions) that volunteers wrote in their own words.

raw_evidence.label: Yearly volume: 1,600x growth from 2015 to 2025
raw_evidence.content: Logged repairs grew from 28 in 2015 (the dashboard's first year) to 45,165 in 2025 — a 1,613x increase. Growth was steady through 2019 (15,491 logs), dropped to 6,686 in 2020 and 5,813 in 2021 (COVID closed cafes physically), then rebounded in 2022 (15,096) and accelerated to 29,406 (2023), 39,981 (2024), and 45,165 (2025). The 2026 figure of 7,346 reflects only the first eight months. The reach of the Repair Cafe movement, in other words, is a hockey stick — the data underestimates the early years because the dashboard didn't exist yet.

Great Britain follows with 21.1% (37,692), France with 11.0% (19,724), Canada 4.3%, Australia 4.0%. Together the top five countries account for 91.2% of all rows. Twenty other countries split the remaining 8.8%, with several (IE, IT, FI, NZ) having only a few hundred rows each. The Dutch over-representation is a major caveat for any global claim — Dutch coffee culture (the Senseo) almost certainly biases the 'most-repaired item' rankings.

raw_evidence.label: EU Right to Repair Directive 2024/1799
raw_evidence.content: The European Union adopted Directive 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods on 30 May 2024; it entered into force 30 July 2024 and member states must transpose it into national law by 31 July 2026 — three months after the most recent rows in this dataset. The directive obliges manufacturers of covered products (washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners, smartphones, etc.) to offer repair within reasonable time and price, prohibits hardware/software anti-repair techniques 'unless objectively justified', and extends the legal sales guarantee by one year when consumers choose repair over replacement. Critics including a 2024 ScienceDirect critical assessment argue the directive still fails to address planned obsolescence head-on, the limited availability of repair manuals, or affordable spare parts. The Repair Cafe data is the largest community-collected ground truth on what actually breaks in European homes, and is increasingly cited by EU policy advocates.

raw_evidence.label: Vacuum cleaner — the most-fought battle (10,284 attempts, 61% saved)
raw_evidence.content: The vacuum cleaner is one of the two most-presented items (10,284 attempts) and ends up repaired in 61.0% of cases. For the 4,021 failed attempts, the largest blocker is 'No way to fix the product' (301 cases, 7.5%), followed closely by 'Spare parts not available at repair session' (292; 7.3%), 'Spare parts too expensive' (240; 6.0%), 'Too worn out' (239; 5.9%), and 'Unidentified failure' (156; 3.9%). 'No way to open the product' was tagged in 153 cases — modern vacuums increasingly use plastic clips and proprietary screws that resist amateur disassembly. Vacuum repair, in short, is a fight against parts availability and design accessibility.
raw_evidence.code:
all_reasons = []
for s in vc_failed['failure_reasons'].dropna().astype(str):
    parts = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r'[;|]', s) if p.strip() and p.strip().upper() != 'NA']
    all_reasons.extend(parts)
rc = Counter(all_reasons)
print("Top failure reasons for vacuum cleaners:")
for r, c in sorted(rc.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:10]:
    print(f"  {c:>5} ({100*c/len(vc_failed):5.2f}%) {r}")

# --- ana_22: Cumulative repairs and CO2 saved (det_03 anchor) ---
print("\n=== ana_22 ===")
df_yes = df[df['repaired'] == 'yes']
total_yes = len(df_yes)
total_co2_kg = total_yes * 24

raw_evidence.label: Top failure reasons: it's the parts, stupid
raw_evidence.content: Across the 65,999 failed-or-half-repaired records, volunteers selected from a checkbox list of failure reason tags. raw_evidence.label: Where the parts run out: electric tools and household electrics top the spare-parts blocker
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to records flagged with a spare-parts failure tag, electric tools have the highest spare-parts blocker rate at 8.3% of all attempts (and 18.0% of all failed attempts in that category). Household appliances electric is second at 7.4% of attempts (16.5% of failed). Display and sound equipment is third at 6.3% / 11.7%. Textile, by contrast, has spare-parts blockers in only 0.5% of attempts — needles and thread are universally available. The pattern aligns with EU Right-to-Repair concerns: it is consumer electronics, not clothing or hand tools, where manufacturers' control of spare parts most directly translates into items being thrown away.
raw_evidence.code:
no_part_by_cat = df.groupby('category').agg(
    failed=('repaired', lambda x: (x.isin(['no','half'])).sum()),
    no_part=('_no_part','sum'),
    n=('repair_id','count')
).reset_index()
no_part_by_cat['no_part_pct_of_failed'] = 100*no_part_by_cat['no_part']/no_part_by_cat['failed'].replace(0, np.nan)
no_part_by_cat['no_part_pct_of_n'] = 100*no_part_by_cat['no_part']/no_part_by_cat['n']
print(no_part_by_cat.sort_values('no_part_pct_of_n', ascending=False).round(2).to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_15: Repairability (1-10) → success rate correlation ---
print("\n=== ana_15 ===")
have = df.dropna(subset=['repairability']).copy()
have['success'] = (have['repaired'] == 'yes').astype(int)
by_score = have.groupby('repairability').agg(success_rate=('success','mean'), n=('success','size')).reset_index()
by_score['success_rate'] *= 100
print(by_score.round(2).to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: EU Right to Repair Directive 2024/1799
raw_evidence.content: The European Union adopted Directive 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods on 30 May 2024; it entered into force 30 July 2024 and member states must transpose it into national law by 31 July 2026 — three months after the most recent rows in this dataset. The directive obliges manufacturers of covered products (washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners, smartphones, etc.) to offer repair within reasonable time and price, prohibits hardware/software anti-repair techniques 'unless objectively justified', and extends the legal sales guarantee by one year when consumers choose repair over replacement. Critics including a 2024 ScienceDirect critical assessment argue the directive still fails to address planned obsolescence head-on, the limited availability of repair manuals, or affordable spare parts. The Repair Cafe data is the largest community-collected ground truth on what actually breaks in European homes, and is increasingly cited by EU policy advocates.

raw_evidence.label: Top failure reasons: it's the parts, stupid
raw_evidence.content: Across the 65,999 failed-or-half-repaired records, volunteers selected from a checkbox list of failure reason tags. The most common tag is 'No way to fix the product' (5,544 cases, 8.4% of failures), followed by 'Spare parts not available at repair session' (4,694; 7.1%), 'Unidentified failure' (3,662; 5.5%), 'Too worn out' (3,341; 5.1%), and 'No way to open the product' (2,305; 3.5%). Spare-parts problems collectively (parts not available at session, not on market, or too expensive) account for 9,042 tags — the single largest barrier when grouped. This data confirms the foundation's earlier 2018 finding that parts availability is the dominant blocker and supports the EU Right-to-Repair argument that manufacturers must make spares accessible.

    parts = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r'[;|]', s) if p.strip() and p.strip().upper() != 'NA']
    all_reasons.extend(parts)
reason_counts = Counter(all_reasons)
total_failed = len(failed)
print(f"Total failed/half rows: {total_failed}")
print(f"Top 15 failure reason tags:")
for r, c in sorted(reason_counts.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:15]:
    print(f"  {c:>6} ({100*c/total_failed:5.1f}%) {r}")

These three buckets sum to roughly 80% of all failed cases — meaning the analyst's free-text NLP work on `failure_reason_open` and `failure_reasons` should expect parts-availability and economic-blocker themes to dominate. Anything outside that envelope (e.g. user-error patterns, brand-specific weak points, software locks) is a story.

raw_evidence.label: Top failure reasons: it's the parts, stupid
raw_evidence.content: Across the 65,999 failed-or-half-repaired records, volunteers selected from a checkbox list of failure reason tags. The most common tag is 'No way to fix the product' (5,544 cases, 8.4% of failures), followed by 'Spare parts not available at repair session' (4,694; 7.1%), 'Unidentified failure' (3,662; 5.5%), 'Too worn out' (3,341; 5.1%), and 'No way to open the product' (2,305; 3.5%). Spare-parts problems collectively (parts not available at session, not on market, or too expensive) account for 9,042 tags — the single largest barrier when grouped. This data confirms the foundation's earlier 2018 finding that parts availability is the dominant blocker and supports the EU Right-to-Repair argument that manufacturers must make spares accessible.

raw_evidence.label: Planned obsolescence: the cultural backdrop
raw_evidence.content: Planned obsolescence is the design strategy of building products with artificially short lifespans — through fragile components, software-locked spare parts, glued-shut shells, or proprietary screws — so that consumers replace rather than repair. It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.label: Brand of vacuum/coffee-maker matters: Dyson at the bottom
raw_evidence.content: Holding product type constant, brand-level success rates vary by 22 percentage points. For vacuum cleaners (n>=100 brand subset), Henry leads at 69.2% success, with Miele 66.0%, Siemens 65.4%, Philips 64.8%, AEG 63.1%. Dyson sits at the bottom at 47.4% (n=1,202) — a brand widely associated with premium price and proprietary design. For coffee makers, Philips (the Senseo manufacturer) leads at 59.5% (n=3,343), followed by Saeco 57.1% and De'Longhi 55.5%. Bosch coffee makers are the worst at 39.0% and Braun the worst overall at 30.9%. Sample sizes here are large enough that the cross-brand spread is unlikely to be noise — though all branding analysis is volunteer-spelled and Dyson units may also skew newer (and harder to open).
raw_evidence.code:
print(g[['brand','n','success_pct']].round(2).to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_17: Country-level success rate ---
print("\n=== ana_17 ===")
g = df.groupby('country').agg(n=('repair_id','count'),
                                yes=('repaired', lambda x:(x=='yes').sum()),
                                half=('repaired', lambda x:(x=='half').sum())).reset_index()
g = g[g['n'] >= 100]
g['success_pct'] = 100*g['yes']/g['n']
g['success_or_partial_pct'] = 100*(g['yes']+g['half'])/g['n']
g = g.sort_values('success_pct', ascending=False)
print(g.round(2).to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Item-age vs success: a U-shape, with old items doing surprisingly well
raw_evidence.content: Plotting success rate against estimated item age reveals a U-shape. New items (0-1 years old) succeed 67.1% of the time — often simple defects under warranty issue. Then success drops to a trough around 6-10 years (55.9%) and 11-15 years (56.6%) — items with worn motors, dead capacitors, no spare parts. Then it rises again: 21-30 years 61.1%, 31-50 years 62.0%, 50+ years 63.2%. The vintage rebound makes physical sense: old items (sewing machines, clocks, radios) were built before planned obsolescence took hold, with replaceable parts and accessible internals. The dataset has 14,112 items aged 20+ years, dominated by sewing machines (1,212), clocks (553), vacuum cleaners (483), radios (471), and turntables (356).
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_18 ===")
df['age'] = df['repair_date'].dt.year - df['estimated_year_of_production']
df_age = df[(df['age'] >= 0) & (df['age'] <= 80)].copy()
print(f"Median age: {df_age['age'].median()}")
print(f"Mean age: {df_age['age'].mean():.2f}")
# Bucket
bins = [-1, 1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 81]
labels = ['0-1','2-3','4-5','6-10','11-15','16-20','21-30','31-50','50+']
df_age['age_bucket'] = pd.cut(df_age['age'], bins=bins, labels=labels)
by_bucket = df_age.groupby('age_bucket', observed=True).agg(
    n=('age','size'),
    success=('repaired', lambda x: (x=='yes').sum())
).reset_index()
by_bucket['success_pct'] = 100*by_bucket['success']/by_bucket['n']
print(by_bucket.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Planned obsolescence: the cultural backdrop
raw_evidence.content: Planned obsolescence is the design strategy of building products with artificially short lifespans — through fragile components, software-locked spare parts, glued-shut shells, or proprietary screws — so that consumers replace rather than repair. It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.label: Vintage items: 14,112 objects aged 20+ brought back from the dead
raw_evidence.content: Items aged 20 years or older — meaning they were built in or before the early 2000s — were brought to Repair Cafes 14,112 times, and 61.6% were successfully repaired. The categories that anchor this vintage flow are sewing machines (1,212 cases), clocks (553), vacuum cleaners (483), radios (471), turntables/record players (356), table lamps (340), and bicycles (331). These are the icons of pre-throwaway design: items that were expensive enough to be worth fixing, simple enough to be opened, and built with parts that are still findable. Vintage textile and lighting items in particular have very high success rates.

raw_evidence.content: Plotting success rate against estimated item age reveals a U-shape. New items (0-1 years old) succeed 67.1% of the time — often simple defects under warranty issue. Then success drops to a trough around 6-10 years (55.9%) and 11-15 years (56.6%) — items with worn motors, dead capacitors, no spare parts. Then it rises again: 21-30 years 61.1%, 31-50 years 62.0%, 50+ years 63.2%. The vintage rebound makes physical sense: old items (sewing machines, clocks, radios) were built before planned obsolescence took hold, with replaceable parts and accessible internals. Source: RepairMonitor dashboard provides insight into repair data (https://www.repaircafe.org/en/repairmonitor-dashboard-provides-insight-into-repa) Facts: Dashboard's eight visualizations focus on product mix, brand mix, cafes, and failure reasons

raw_evidence.label: Scope suggestion: the analyst's targets
raw_evidence.content: Five quantitative directions are most worth time. (1) Product mix: top 15 kind_of_product items by frequency, broken into repaired/half/no — the canonical 'what breaks most' chart. (2) Repairability ratings by product and category — does the volunteer 1-10 score line up with success rate? (3) Brand-level survival: which brands of coffee maker, vacuum, smartphone are most repairable? Beware sample-size bias. (4) Geography: 25 countries but Netherlands dominates (>50% of rows) — split NL vs rest of world to avoid Dutch coffee-machine bias. (5) Free-text mining: tokenize defect_found and failure_reason_open, surface the most common defect verbs ('does not turn on', 'leaks', 'no power') and the most common failure-reason phrases. (6) Information sources: filter `repair_info_source` for YouTube vs ChatGPT/AI mentions over time — the dataset goes through 2026 so there is enough runway to see GenAI rising. Caveats to watch: NL-Dutch dominance, lots of NA values in repairability when failure occurred, free-text fields are multilingual (Dutch, French, English).

raw_evidence.label: GenAI vs YouTube as repair information sources
raw_evidence.content: Volunteers can record where they got repair information. YouTube has been the dominant external source since 2017, but its share has plateaued: 0.3% in 2017, 0.5% in 2023, 0.4% in 2026 (early). Generative AI is a brand-new entrant — zero mentions before 2023 — but is rising fast on a relative basis: 2 mentions in 2023, 8 in 2024, 14 in 2025, and 2 in the partial 2026 sample. The earliest unambiguous AI mention is 9 September 2023 ('chat gpt' for an unspecified item). Examples of how volunteers logged it include 'chat gpt', 'WWW.OPENai.COM', 'chatgpt', 'AI Perplexity', 'perplexity et manuel', and even an OpenAI conversation share URL. While AI mentions remain a tiny fraction of total rows (26 cumulatively versus 843 YouTube mentions), the trajectory in this dataset is the first traceable evidence in volunteer repair logs of a new tool entering the fixer's toolkit.
raw_evidence.code:
url['repair_info_url_l'] = url['repair_info_url'].astype(str).str.lower()

# Tag types
def tag_source(s):
    if 'youtube' in s or 'youtu.be' in s:
        return 'youtube'
    if any(k in s for k in ['chatgpt','chat gpt','openai','gpt-','gemini','bard','claude','copilot','perplexity','grok','generative ai','gen ai','genai','ai ','ai,','artificial intelligence']):
        return 'genai'
    if 'manual' in s or 'handleiding' in s or 'instruction' in s or 'guide' in s or 'service manual' in s:
        return 'manual'
    if 'ifixit' in s:
        return 'ifixit'
    if 'forum' in s or 'reddit' in s:
        return 'forum'
    if 'website' in s or 'site' in s or 'http' in s or 'www' in s or '.com' in s or '.nl' in s:
        return 'other_web'
    if 'experience' in s or 'own knowledge' in s or 'eigen' in s or 'expert' in s:
        return 'experience'
    if 'colleague' in s or 'collega' in s or 'friend' in s:
        return 'colleague'
    return 'other'

# Combine source + url evidence
df['_src'] = df['repair_info_source'].astype(str).str.lower().fillna('')
df['_url'] = df['repair_info_url'].astype(str).str.lower().fillna('')
df['_combo'] = df['_src'] + ' || ' + df['_url']

raw_evidence.label: GenAI vs YouTube as repair information sources
raw_evidence.content: Volunteers can record where they got repair information. YouTube has been the dominant external source since 2017, but its share has plateaued: 0.3% in 2017, 0.5% in 2023, 0.4% in 2026 (early). Generative AI is a brand-new entrant — zero mentions before 2023 — but is rising fast on a relative basis: 2 mentions in 2023, 8 in 2024, 14 in 2025, and 2 in the partial 2026 sample. The earliest unambiguous AI mention is 9 September 2023 ('chat gpt' for an unspecified item). Examples of how volunteers logged it include 'chat gpt', 'WWW.OPENai.COM', 'chatgpt', 'AI Perplexity', 'perplexity et manuel', and even an OpenAI conversation share URL. While AI mentions remain a tiny fraction of total rows (26 cumulatively versus 843 YouTube mentions), the trajectory in this dataset is the first traceable evidence in volunteer repair logs of a new tool entering the fixer's toolkit.
raw_evidence.code:
url['repair_info_url_l'] = url['repair_info_url'].astype(str).str.lower()

# Tag types
def tag_source(s):
    if 'youtube' in s or 'youtu.be' in s:
        return 'youtube'
    if any(k in s for k in ['chatgpt','chat gpt','openai','gpt-','gemini','bard','claude','copilot','perplexity','grok','generative ai','gen ai','genai','ai ','ai,','artificial intelligence']):
        return 'genai'
    if 'manual' in s or 'handleiding' in s or 'instruction' in s or 'guide' in s or 'service manual' in s:
        return 'manual'
    if 'ifixit' in s:
        return 'ifixit'
    if 'forum' in s or 'reddit' in s:
        return 'forum'
    if 'website' in s or 'site' in s or 'http' in s or 'www' in s or '.com' in s or '.nl' in s:
        return 'other_web'
    if 'experience' in s or 'own knowledge' in s or 'eigen' in s or 'expert' in s:
        return 'experience'
    if 'colleague' in s or 'collega' in s or 'friend' in s:
        return 'colleague'
    return 'other'

# Combine source + url evidence
df['_src'] = df['repair_info_source'].astype(str).str.lower().fillna('')
df['_url'] = df['repair_info_url'].astype(str).str.lower().fillna('')
df['_combo'] = df['_src'] + ' || ' + df['_url']

ai_pat = r'(chatgpt|chat\s*gpt|openai|\bgpt[- ]?[345o]|gemini|bard\b|claude|copilot|perplexity|\bgrok\b|generative\s*ai|\bgen[- ]?ai\b|artificial\s*intelligence)'
yt_pat = r'(youtube|youtu\.be)'

df['_is_ai'] = df['_combo'].str.contains(ai_pat, regex=True, na=False)
df['_is_yt'] = df['_combo'].str.contains(yt_pat, regex=True, na=False)
# A row 'used some info' if used_repair_info=='yes' or any source/url filled
df['_used_info'] = (df['used_repair_info'].astype(str).str.lower() == 'yes') | (df['repair_info_source'].notna()) | (df['repair_info_url'].notna())

print(f"Total rows: {len(df)}")
print(f"Rows with AI mention: {df['_is_ai'].sum()}")
print(f"Rows with YouTube mention: {df['_is_yt'].sum()}")

# By year
yr = df.groupby('year').agg(
    n=('repair_id','count'),
    used=('_used_info','sum'),
    yt=('_is_yt','sum'),
    ai=('_is_ai','sum')
).reset_index()
yr['yt_pct'] = 100*yr['yt']/yr['n']
yr['ai_pct'] = 100*yr['ai']/yr['n']
print(yr.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Planned obsolescence: the cultural backdrop
raw_evidence.content: Planned obsolescence is the design strategy of building products with artificially short lifespans — through fragile components, software-locked spare parts, glued-shut shells, or proprietary screws — so that consumers replace rather than repair. It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.label: Trousers — the textile success champion (96.0%)
raw_evidence.content: Trousers and pants account for 6,769 logged repairs, the third largest item category, and they are repaired 96.0% of the time. The dominant defect is 'te lang' (Dutch: too long, 615 cases) — i.e., people bring in trousers to be hemmed, not because they are broken. Other top defects are 'korter maken' (make shorter, 195), 'pijpen te lang' (legs too long, 99), 'too long' (87), 'is te lang' (71), 'scheur' (tear, 64), 'naad los' (loose seam, 61), 'rits kapot' (broken zipper, 53), 'torn' (41), and 'zoom los' (loose hem, 39). The data exposes something subtle: a large share of 'repair' work at Repair Cafes is in fact alteration — adapting clothing to fit a body, not fixing a fault. This category alone is responsible for the textile category's very high success rate.

raw_evidence.label: Success rate by product type — knives and trousers thrive, kettles and printers don't
raw_evidence.content: Repair success varies wildly by item. The clear winners are non-electric, mechanical items: knives/scissors are repaired 97.5% of the time (mostly sharpening), trousers/pants 96.0%, garden shears 95.4%, coats/jackets 89.7%, and bicycles 84.1%. The clear losers are electronics with sealed components or cheap consumer-grade builds: electric kettles succeed only 39.9% (50.9% are unfixable), printers 36.8% (42.2% unfixable), irons 49.4%, food processors 49.1%, laptops 49.7%, toasters 51.1%, and coffee makers 50.6%. The data tells a story: the more electronic the item, the less likely it can be saved.

ct = pd.crosstab(sub['kind_of_product'], sub['repaired'], normalize='index') * 100
ct = ct.reindex(top20)
ct['n'] = repairs['kind_of_product'].value_counts().reindex(top20).values
print(ct.round(1).to_string())

print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
country_counts = repairs['country'].value_counts()

sentences.summary: det_08: Why a general reader cares: anti-consumerism in microcosm. Source: About Repair Cafe (https://www.repaircafe.org/en/about/) Facts: Repair Cafes provide free help to fix broken household items in a community setting

raw_evidence.label: Why a general reader cares: anti-consumerism in microcosm
raw_evidence.content: The Repair Cafe row-level data offers something a press release cannot: a granular, volunteer-collected ledger of which specific objects in twenty-five countries refused to be thrown away. Each row carries a small political statement (someone chose to fix instead of buy) but also a quiet failure mode (sometimes the object refused to be fixed). That tension — repair as virtue, planned obsolescence as opponent — is where the story spine lives. The 'why is it broken' free text is especially rare: industrial repair statistics usually come from manufacturer warranty data, which excludes anything out of warranty and never records what the user thinks happened. Repair Cafe data does both. Translating one repair into ~24 kg of avoided CO2 (det_03) and the EU's new Right-to-Repair regime (det_04) gives the reader two reasons the numbers matter beyond Saturday-afternoon hobbyism.

raw_evidence.label: Verbatim 'we couldn't fix it' quotes — the human-language texture
raw_evidence.content: The free-text failure_reason_open field captures, in volunteers' own words, the tiny tragedies that show up when a thing cannot be fixed. A sample includes: 'product is van inferieure kwaliteit, slecht te repareren' (Coffee maker — 'product is of inferior quality, badly repairable'), 'Vital Component Failure. Not available to purchase.' (Printer), 'Het apparaat is te oud om nog te repareren' (Laptop — 'the device is too old to be repaired'), 'Onderdeel is niet te vervangen' (Display monitor — 'part cannot be replaced'), 'electronicafout op de print (geen schema)' (Video player — 'electronics fault on the board, no circuit diagram'), 'Schema nodig, niet te vinden' (Radio — 'circuit diagram needed, cannot be found'), 'versterker heeft computer die alles checkt, maar wil niet starten, ook vol sigarenrook' (Amplifier — 'amp has a computer that checks everything but won't start, also full of cigar smoke'). These quotes show the dataset's ethnographic value: each row is a small story about a specific object meeting a specific obstacle.
raw_evidence.code:
if s.upper() == s: return False
    if s.lower() in ['na','n/a']: return False
    return True
quotes_pool['ok'] = quotes_pool['fr_open'].apply(good_q)
sample = quotes_pool[quotes_pool['ok']].sample(40, random_state=7)
print("Random failure_reason_open quotes (n=40):")
for _, row in sample.iterrows():
    print(f"  [{row['kind_of_product']}] {row['fr_open'][:180]}")

# --- ana_24: Most common 'suggestions' phrases (advice from repairers) ---

top_sug = sug.value_counts().head(20)
print("Top 20 suggestion phrases:")

raw_evidence.label: Why a general reader cares: anti-consumerism in microcosm
raw_evidence.content: The Repair Cafe row-level data offers something a press release cannot: a granular, volunteer-collected ledger of which specific objects in twenty-five countries refused to be thrown away. Each row carries a small political statement (someone chose to fix instead of buy) but also a quiet failure mode (sometimes the object refused to be fixed). That tension — repair as virtue, planned obsolescence as opponent — is where the story spine lives. The 'why is it broken' free text is especially rare: industrial repair statistics usually come from manufacturer warranty data, which excludes anything out of warranty and never records what the user thinks happened. Repair Cafe data does both. Translating one repair into ~24 kg of avoided CO2 (det_03) and the EU's new Right-to-Repair regime (det_04) gives the reader two reasons the numbers matter beyond Saturday-afternoon hobbyism.

raw_evidence.label: Carbon: one repair prevents about 24 kg of CO2
raw_evidence.content: British researcher Steve Privett (University of Surrey, master's degree work) developed the Repair Cafe Foundation's carbon estimation method. Their headline figure is that one product successfully repaired at a Repair Cafe prevents roughly 24 kilograms of CO2 emissions, mostly avoided by not manufacturing a replacement. Scaled up, the foundation estimates the global Repair Cafe network could save over 8.5 million kilograms of CO2 per year if all branches were active. In 2019 alone, 420,000 successful repairs across 2,000 active cafes prevented up to 10 million kilograms of CO2. The Farnham Repair Cafe (UK) released a free Repair Cafe Carbon Calculator in 2024 so cafes can compute their own carbon savings — translating, for example, 35 kg of repaired electrical items into 306 kg of avoided CO2, equivalent to 191 hot showers. This is the climate frame for any 'repair vs replace' finding the analyst surfaces.

raw_evidence.content: The European Union adopted Directive 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods on 30 May 2024; it entered into force 30 July 2024 and member states must transpose it into national law by 31 July 2026 — three months after the most recent rows in this dataset. The directive obliges manufacturers of covered products (washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners, smartphones, etc.) to offer repair within reasonable time and price, prohibits hardware/software anti-repair techniques 'unless objectively justified', and extends the legal sales guarantee by one year when consumers choose repair over replacement. Critics including a 2024 ScienceDirect critical assessment argue the directive still fails to address planned obsolescence head-on, the limited availability of repair manuals, or affordable spare parts. The Repair Cafe data is the largest community-collected ground truth on what actually breaks in European homes, and is increasingly cited by EU policy advocates.

raw_evidence.label: Carbon: one repair prevents about 24 kg of CO2
raw_evidence.content: British researcher Steve Privett (University of Surrey, master's degree work) developed the Repair Cafe Foundation's carbon estimation method. Their headline figure is that one product successfully repaired at a Repair Cafe prevents roughly 24 kilograms of CO2 emissions, mostly avoided by not manufacturing a replacement. Scaled up, the foundation estimates the global Repair Cafe network could save over 8.5 million kilograms of CO2 per year if all branches were active. In 2019 alone, 420,000 successful repairs across 2,000 active cafes prevented up to 10 million kilograms of CO2. The Farnham Repair Cafe (UK) released a free Repair Cafe Carbon Calculator in 2024 so cafes can compute their own carbon savings — translating, for example, 35 kg of repaired electrical items into 306 kg of avoided CO2, equivalent to 191 hot showers. This is the climate frame for any 'repair vs replace' finding the analyst surfaces.

raw_evidence.content: The European Union adopted Directive 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods on 30 May 2024; it entered into force 30 July 2024 and member states must transpose it into national law by 31 July 2026 — three months after the most recent rows in this dataset. The directive obliges manufacturers of covered products (washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners, smartphones, etc.) to offer repair within reasonable time and price, prohibits hardware/software anti-repair techniques 'unless objectively justified', and extends the legal sales guarantee by one year when consumers choose repair over replacement. Critics including a 2024 ScienceDirect critical assessment argue the directive still fails to address planned obsolescence head-on, the limited availability of repair manuals, or affordable spare parts. The Repair Cafe data is the largest community-collected ground truth on what actually breaks in European homes, and is increasingly cited by EU policy advocates.

raw_evidence.content: British researcher Steve Privett (University of Surrey, master's degree work) developed the Repair Cafe Foundation's carbon estimation method. Their headline figure is that one product successfully repaired at a Repair Cafe prevents roughly 24 kilograms of CO2 emissions, mostly avoided by not manufacturing a replacement. Scaled up, the foundation estimates the global Repair Cafe network could save over 8.5 million kilograms of CO2 per year if all branches were active. In 2019 alone, 420,000 successful repairs across 2,000 active cafes prevented up to 10 million kilograms of CO2. The Farnham Repair Cafe (UK) released a free Repair Cafe Carbon Calculator in 2024 so cafes can compute their own carbon savings — translating, for example, 35 kg of repaired electrical items into 306 kg of avoided CO2, equivalent to 191 hot showers. This is the climate frame for any 'repair vs replace' finding the analyst surfaces.

raw_evidence.label: Carbon: one repair prevents about 24 kg of CO2
raw_evidence.content: British researcher Steve Privett (University of Surrey, master's degree work) developed the Repair Cafe Foundation's carbon estimation method. Their headline figure is that one product successfully repaired at a Repair Cafe prevents roughly 24 kilograms of CO2 emissions, mostly avoided by not manufacturing a replacement. Scaled up, the foundation estimates the global Repair Cafe network could save over 8.5 million kilograms of CO2 per year if all branches were active. In 2019 alone, 420,000 successful repairs across 2,000 active cafes prevented up to 10 million kilograms of CO2. The Farnham Repair Cafe (UK) released a free Repair Cafe Carbon Calculator in 2024 so cafes can compute their own carbon savings — translating, for example, 35 kg of repaired electrical items into 306 kg of avoided CO2, equivalent to 191 hot showers. This is the climate frame for any 'repair vs replace' finding the analyst surfaces.

raw_evidence.label: EU Right to Repair Directive 2024/1799
raw_evidence.content: The European Union adopted Directive 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods on 30 May 2024; it entered into force 30 July 2024 and member states must transpose it into national law by 31 July 2026 — three months after the most recent rows in this dataset. The directive obliges manufacturers of covered products (washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners, smartphones, etc.) to offer repair within reasonable time and price, prohibits hardware/software anti-repair techniques 'unless objectively justified', and extends the legal sales guarantee by one year when consumers choose repair over replacement. Critics including a 2024 ScienceDirect critical assessment argue the directive still fails to address planned obsolescence head-on, the limited availability of repair manuals, or affordable spare parts. The Repair Cafe data is the largest community-collected ground truth on what actually breaks in European homes, and is increasingly cited by EU policy advocates.

raw_evidence.label: Cumulative CO2 saved: 2,707 tonnes from this dataset alone
raw_evidence.content: Applying the Repair Cafe Foundation's 24-kg-CO2-per-successful-repair benchmark from det_03, the 112,776 successful repairs in this dataset prevented an estimated 2,707 tonnes of CO2 emissions from manufacturing replacements. The cumulative trajectory mirrors the activity volume: 1 tonne by 2015, 213 tonnes by 2018, 547 tonnes by 2020, 1,287 tonnes by 2023, 2,594 tonnes by 2025, 2,708 tonnes by August 2026. This is one community sample — the foundation's network-wide estimate is far larger.

raw_evidence.label: Planned obsolescence: the cultural backdrop
raw_evidence.content: Planned obsolescence is the design strategy of building products with artificially short lifespans — through fragile components, software-locked spare parts, glued-shut shells, or proprietary screws — so that consumers replace rather than repair. It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.

raw_evidence.label: Repairability score is a strong predictor of success
raw_evidence.content: There is a clear monotonic relationship between volunteer repairability rating and outcome. Items rated 1 ('difficult') are repaired only 13.7% of the time. The success rate climbs almost linearly to 56.9% at score 5, then 78.4% at 8, 84.9% at 9, and 85.8% at 10. The fact that even score-10 items fail 14% of the time tells you something else — sometimes a fixable item is not actually fixed because the volunteer ran out of time, lacked a part on the day, or the visitor never came back to collect the result. The score itself is a useful, internally-consistent signal of design quality.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_16 ===")
# Restrict to one common product type for fairness: Vacuum cleaners
for product in ['Vacuum cleaner', 'Coffee maker']:
    sub = df[df['kind_of_product'] == product]
    g = sub.groupby('brand').agg(n=('repair_id','count'), yes=('repaired', lambda x: (x=='yes').sum())).reset_index()
    g = g[g['n'] >= 100]
    g['success_pct'] = 100*g['yes']/g['n']
    g = g.sort_values('success_pct', ascending=False)

It surfaces in this dataset as the most common failure reason recorded by Repair Cafe volunteers: 'spare parts not available' and 'damage to the device cannot be repaired'. The repairability column (1 = difficult, 10 = easy) is essentially a volunteer-given anti-obsolescence rating. The Repair Cafe movement positions itself explicitly as a counter-narrative to throwaway consumer culture, with Postma framing it as a way to 'reignite the do-it-together and do-it-yourself spirit'. This frames the analyst's job: each unrepairable record is a small piece of evidence about a specific product that resisted being fixed.
